
# 1. Project Overview

This project focuses on preparing property and sales data for a house price prediction analysis. The goal is to create a clean and meaningful dataset that can later be used for exploratory data analysis, feature selection, and predictive modeling.

The analysis combines several property-related data sources, including sales transactions, appraisal account information, property improvements, building characteristics, land attributes, parcel history, and tax account information.

# 2. Setup and Required Libraries

This section loads the R packages required for data loading, data manipulation, text processing, categorical association analysis, correlation analysis, and data reshaping.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(rcompanion)
library(corrplot)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(lubridate)
library(gridExtra)

```

# 3. Data Sources

The following section presents a detailed review of each data source, focusing on the information it contains, its structure, and its potential relevance for the analysis.

Each original text file is loaded separately and assigned meaningful column names based on the official data documentation. Since the raw files do not contain column headers, assigning column names is an important first step before any analysis can be performed.

## 3.1 Sales Table

The **Sale** table contains information about recorded property transactions, including when a sale occurred, the recorded sale price, and the parcels involved in the transaction. It also includes fields that help evaluate whether a sale is valid, verified, or excluded from official sales analysis.

```{r}
sale_df <- read_delim("C:/Users/Gerta Hajrullahi/Desktop/MDS/SS26/Solution Eng/Project/datasources/sale.txt",delim = "|")
colnames(sale_df) <- c(
  "etn",                    # (PK) used to identify a sale transaction; may repeat if one recorded sale includes multiple parcels 
  "parcel_count",           # nr of parcels associated with a sale
  "parcel_number",          # (PK) unique 10 digit nr assigned to each property 
  "sale_date",              # date the legal document was executed
  "sale_price",             # dollar amount recorded on the ETN
  "deep_type",              # tells what legal document was used to transfer or record ownership/interest in the property
  "grantor",                # people/company giving/transferring ownership rights (seller)
  "grantee",                # people/company getting ownership rights (buyer)
  "valid_invalid",          # valid sale represents a normal market value; invalid sale is a sale that may not reflect the true market value of the property (gifts, sales between relatives etc.)
  "confirmed_unconfirmed",  # shows if the property details and sale circumstances were correct/verifies at the time of sale
  "exclude_reason",         # explains why a sale was excluded from official sales analysis, such as family transfers, forced sales, estate sales, or property changes after the sale
  "improved_vacant",        # shows whether the sale includes a parcel with building value, or whether it is vacant land with no building value
  "appraisal_account_type"  # describes how the parcel is classified
)
```

## 3.2 Appraisal Account Table

The **Appraisal Account** table contains parcel-level appraisal information, including parcel classification, land size, utility availability, street access, appraisal date, and location coordinates.

This table provides important parcel characteristics that may help explain differences in property prices.

```{r}
appraisal_account_df <- read_delim("C:/Users/Gerta Hajrullahi/Desktop/MDS/SS26/Solution Eng/Project/datasources/appraisal_account.txt",delim = "|")
colnames(appraisal_account_df) <- c(
  "parcel_number",              # (PK) unique 10 digit number assigned to each property
  "appraisal_account_type",     # describes how a parcel is classified
  "business_name",              # main business name on the parcel or space number for a mobile/manufactured home in a park
  "value_area_id",              # identifies the physical inspection cycle for each parcel
  "land_economic_area",         # code that ties parcels to land valuation models or appraisal location areas
  "buildings",                  # number of improvements/buildings located on a parcel
  "group_account_number",       # ties parcels qualifying for valuation as one economic unit or condominium project
  "land_gross_acres",           # total acres that make up the economic unit, which may include multiple parcels
  "land_net_acres",             # size of the individual parcel in acres
  "land_gross_square_feet",     # total square feet that make up the economic unit, which may include multiple parcels
  "land_net_square_feet",       # size of the individual parcel in square feet
  "land_gross_front_feet",      # front feet of the site, lot, or effective waterfront length depending on parcel type
  "land_width",                 # residential use only; effective waterfront front feet for the parcel or group
  "land_depth",                 # residential use only; effective waterfront depth for the parcel or group
  "submerged_area_square_feet", # area of a parcel that is submerged and not included in gross or net square feet
  "appraisal_date",             # most recent date an appraiser observed the property or changed the record
  "waterfront_type",            # describes the type of waterfront the property adjoins or has legal access to
  "view_quality",               # reflects the market appeal of the overall view available from the dwelling or property
  "utility_electric",           # identifies whether power is installed, available, or not available on the property
  "utility_sewer",              # identifies whether sewer/septic is installed, available, not available, or unsupported
  "utility_water",              # identifies whether water is installed, available, or not available
  "street_type",                # identifies whether the access street is paved or unpaved
  "latitude",                   # latitude of the parcel centroid
  "longitude"                   # longitude of the parcel centroid
)
```

## 3.3 Improvement Table

The **Improvement** table contains information about buildings or improvements located on a parcel.

It includes property type, neighborhood, building size, condition, quality, occupancy type, porch area, garage area, and fireplace information. These features are useful because building characteristics are often strongly related to property value.

```{r}
improvement_df <- read_delim("C:/Users/Gerta Hajrullahi/Desktop/MDS/SS26/Solution Eng/Project/datasources/improvement.txt",delim = "|")
colnames(improvement_df) <- c(
  "parcel_number",                    # (PK) unique 10 digit number assigned to each property
  "building_id",                      # (PK) unique identifier for each improvement record on a parcel
  "property_type",                    # links the building to the proper cost and depreciation tables
  "neighborhood",                     # area with similar social, environmental, economic, and governmental characteristics
  "neighborhood_extension",           # additional neighborhood/use classification based on property type
  "square_feet",                      # total square feet for the built-as types identified for the building
  "net_square_feet",                  # net rentable area for commercial properties; for residential, usually built-as square feet or zero
  "percent_complete",                 # construction completion percentage; completed structures are listed as 100%
  "condition",                        # overall depreciation, maintenance, and upkeep condition of the structure
  "quality",                          # quality of materials, workmanship, architectural attractiveness, and functional design
  "primary_occupancy_code",           # numeric code describing how the improvement is primarily occupied
  "primary_occupancy_description",    # text description of the primary occupancy code
  "mobile_home_serial_number",        # serial number listed on the mobile home title
  "mobile_home_total_length",         # mobile home length in feet from the title or appraiser inspection
  "mobile_home_make",                 # make of the mobile home
  "attic_finished_square_feet",       # finished living area in the attic
  "basement_square_feet",             # total square footage of the basement
  "basement_finished_square_feet",    # finished square footage of the basement
  "carport_square_feet",              # total square footage of all carports
  "balcony_square_feet",              # total square footage of all balcony areas
  "porch_square_feet",                # total square footage associated with all porches
  "attached_garage_square_feet",      # total square footage of attached or built-in garages
  "detached_garage_square_feet",      # total square footage of detached garages
  "fireplaces",                       # total count of fireplaces or prefab stoves
  "basement_garage_door"              # indicates whether basement garage doors are single or double
)
```

```{r}
  "roof_cover",                 # material used for the roof
  "bedrooms",                   # number of bedrooms listed for a residential property
  "bathrooms",                  # number of bathrooms listed as a decimal
  "units",                      # number of separate units within the building
  "class_code",                 # cost group code based on framing, walls, floors, roof structure, and fireproofing
```

# 4. Data Quality Checks

Before joining or analyzing the data, basic data quality checks are performed for each data source.

The purpose of this step is to understand the structure, completeness, and potential quality issues of each table. The checks include the number of rows, number of columns, duplicate rows, total missing values, and number of columns with missing values.

```{r}
# function for data quality checks for each of the dataframes
data_quality_check <- function(df, table_name) {
  missing_by_col <- sapply(df, function(x) {
    
    x_char <- as.character(x)
    
    sum(
      is.na(x) |
        is.na(x_char) |
        x_char == "" |
        x_char == "NA" |
        x_char == " "
    )
  })
  
  data.frame(
    table_name = table_name,
    rows = nrow(df),
    columns = ncol(df),
    duplicate_rows = sum(duplicated(df)),
    total_missing_values = sum(missing_by_col),
    columns_with_missing_values = sum(missing_by_col > 0),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

# list of the dataframes above
metadata_dfs <- list(
  sale = sale_df,
  appraisal_account = appraisal_account_df,
  improvement = improvement_df,
  improvement_builtas = improvement_builtas_df,
  improvement_detail = improvement_detail_df,
  land_attribute = land_attribute_df,
  seg_merge = seg_merge_df,
  tax_account = tax_account_df
)
```

## 4.1 Data Quality Summary

A summary table is created for all data sources. This gives a high-level overview of the size and quality of each table.

```{r}
quality_summary <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(metadata_dfs), function(name) {
    data_quality_check(metadata_dfs[[name]], name)
  })
)

quality_summary
```

From the summary table we can see that there are no duplicates in each of the tables. Columns with missing values will be further inspected.

## 4.2 Parcel Number Check

The parcel number is the main identifier used to connect the different data sources.

This step checks whether `parcel_number` is repeated in each table. Understanding this is important because repeated parcel numbers can create one-to-many or many-to-many relationships during joins.

```{r}
parcel_duplicate_summary <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(metadata_dfs), function(name) {
    df <- metadata_dfs[[name]]
    
    if ("parcel_number" %in% names(df)) {
      data.frame(
        table_name = name,
        rows = nrow(df),
        unique_parcels = n_distinct(df$parcel_number),
        repeated_parcel_rows = nrow(df) - n_distinct(df$parcel_number)
      )
    }
  })
)

parcel_duplicate_summary
```

Tables appraisal_account and tax_account do not have repeated parcel numbers. This will be further investigated if this will cause a problem with joining the datasets.

## 4.3 Missing Values by Column

After the overall missing value summary, missing values are inspected at the column level.

This helps identify columns with very high missingness. Columns with a high percentage of missing values are reviewed and may be excluded from the analysis if they are unlikely to provide reliable information.

```{r}
# function for missing values in each column
missing_by_column <- function(df, table_name) {
  
  data.frame(
    table_name = table_name,
    column_name = names(df),
    missing_count = sapply(df, function(x) sum(is.na(x) | x == "", na.rm = TRUE)),
    missing_percent = round(
      sapply(df, function(x) mean(is.na(x) | x == "", na.rm = TRUE)) * 100,
      2
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}
```

```{r}
missing_summary <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(metadata_dfs), function(name) {
    missing_by_column(metadata_dfs[[name]], name)
  })
)

missing_summary %>%
  filter(missing_count > 0) %>%
  arrange(table_name, desc(missing_percent))
```

# 5. Column Selection Based on Missing Values

Columns with a very high percentage of missing values are removed from selected tables.

The goal of this step is to reduce noise and remove variables that are unlikely to be useful for modeling or interpretation due to lack of data.

From the table above we can see that for appraisal_account columns waterfront_type, view_quality, group_account_number, business_name and submerged_area_square_feet have a high percentage of missing values (over 80%). This is why these columns will not be considered for the analysis.

```{r}
appraisal_account_analysis <- appraisal_account_df %>%

head(appraisal_account_analysis,2)
```

After removing high-missing columns, duplicate checks are repeated on the cleaned data sources.

```{r}
duplicate_summary <- bind_rows(
```

# 7. Sales Filtering

The Sale table is filtered to include only sales that are considered valid and confirmed.

For this analysis, only sales that are marked as valid, confirmed, have no exclusion reason, and have a positive sale price are kept. This helps ensure that the target variable reflects normal market transactions as much as possible.

```{r}
sale_analysis <- sale_df %>%
  filter(
    valid_invalid == 1,
    confirmed_unconfirmed == 1,
    is.na(exclude_reason) | exclude_reason == "",
    !is.na(sale_price),
    sale_price > 0
  )
```

# 8. Joining the Data Sources

The cleaned data sources are joined into one analysis dataset.

The Sale table is used as the base table because it contains the target variable, `sale_price`. Other tables are joined using `parcel_number` and, where applicable, `building_id`.

Because some tables contain multiple records per parcel or building, the join may create repeated rows. This is expected based on the structure of the data.

```{r}
joined_df <- sale_analysis %>%
  left_join(
    appraisal_account_analysis,
    by = "parcel_number",
    suffix = c("_sale", "_appraisal")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    improvement_analysis,
    by = "parcel_number",
    suffix = c("", "_improvement")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    improvement_builtas_analysis,
    by = c("parcel_number", "building_id"),
    suffix = c("", "_builtas")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    improvement_detail_df,
    by = c("parcel_number", "building_id"),
    suffix = c("", "_detail")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    land_attribute_df,
    by = "parcel_number",
    suffix = c("", "_land")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    seg_merge_df,
    by = "parcel_number",
    suffix = c("", "_segmerge")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    tax_account_analysis,
    by = "parcel_number",
    suffix = c("", "_tax")
  )

head(joined_df, 2)
```

```{r}
nrow(joined_df)
```

# 9. Unique Value Analysis

After joining the tables, the number of unique values is checked for each column.

This step helps identify columns with only one unique value, identifier-like columns, columns with very high cardinality, text columns that may need grouping, and variables that may not be useful for predictive modeling.

```{r}
unique_summary_joined <- data.frame(
  column_name = names(joined_df),
  unique_values = sapply(joined_df, function(x) n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

unique_summary_joined %>%
  arrange(desc(unique_values))
```

Columns with only one unique value will be identified, as they do not provide any variability for analysis and can be excluded from the analysis.

```{r}
cols_to_remove <- unique_summary_joined %>%
  filter(unique_values <= 1) %>%
  pull(column_name)

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-all_of(cols_to_remove))
```

Examples include transaction IDs, parcel IDs, building IDs, owner names, address-related fields, and administrative codes.

# 11. Feature Engineering

Feature engineering is performed to simplify complex categorical variables and create more meaningful features for analysis.

Several detailed text variables are grouped into broader categories to make them easier to interpret and more useful for modeling.

## 11.1 Utility and Street Access Grouping

Utility and street access variables are simplified into broader groups.

This includes electric, sewer, water, and street access information. Grouping these values helps reduce category complexity while preserving important information about property usability and accessibility.

```{r}

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    
    utility_sewer = case_when(
      utility_sewer %in% c("SEWER/SEPTIC INSTALLED","SEWER AVAILABLE","SEWER/SEPTIC AVAIL") ~ "Sewer/Septic Available or Installed",
      utility_sewer %in% c("SEWER/SEPTIC NO","SEWER/SEPTIC NO PERC") ~ "No Sewer/Septic",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    utility_water = case_when(
      utility_water %in% c("WATER INSTALLED", "WATER AVAILABLE") ~ "Water Available or Installed",
      utility_water == "WATER NO" ~ "No Water",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    street_type = case_when(
      street_type == "PAVED" ~ "Road Access",
      street_type %in% c("STREET UNPAVED", "STREET NO ROAD") ~ "Limited or No Road Access",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    utility_electric = case_when(
      utility_electric %in% c("POWER INSTALLED", "POWER AVAILABLE") ~ "Power Available or Installed",
      utility_electric == "POWER NO - COMMENT" ~ "No Power",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    primary_occupancy_clean = str_trim(primary_occupancy_description),
    primary_occupancy_group = case_when(
      is.na(primary_occupancy_clean) ~ NA_character_,
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Single Family|Townhouse|Condo|Duplex|Triplex|Apartment|Apt|Residential|Studio Loft|Cabin", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Residential",
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Mobile|Manufactured|MH Park|Title Elim MH", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Mobile Home",
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Office|Bank|Medical|Geriatric|Hospital|Government|School|Education|Religious|Church|Fellowship", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Institutional/Office/Services",
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Retail|Restaurant|Fast Food|C-Store|Gas|Store|Bar|Tavern|Hotel|Motel|Casino|Snack Bar|Auto Dealer|Dealership|Car Wash|Mini Lube|Automotive", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Commercial/Retail/Hospitality",
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Warehouse|Storage|Industrial|Manufacturing|Hangar|Hanger|Flex|Garage|Quonset|Utility|Fuel Tank|Water Tank|Material|Shelter", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Industrial/Storage/Utility",
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Agricultural|Barn|Stable|Horse|Poultry|Kennel", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Agricultural/Outbuilding",
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Parking|Marina|Boat|RV Park|Recreational|Pool|Tennis|Clubhouse", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Recreational/Parking/Other",
      str_detect(primary_occupancy_clean, regex("Addon Only|Imps on", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Improvement Only",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    
    hvac_description_clean = str_trim(hvac_description),
    hvac_group = case_when(
      is.na(hvac_description) ~ NA_character_,
      hvac_description_clean %in% c("Forced Air","Warm and Cool Air Zone","Floor/Wall Furnace","Floor Wall Furnace") ~ "Forced air or furnace",
      hvac_description_clean %in% c("Electric","Electric Baseboard","Electric Wall","Space Heater") ~ "Electric heat", 
      hvac_description_clean %in% c("Heat Pump","Heat Pump Individual Unit") ~ "Heat pump",
      hvac_description_clean %in% c("Hot Water","Hot Water Baseboard","Hot Water Radiant","Hot Chilled Water","Radiant","Steam","Steam w/o Boiler") ~ "Water, steam, or radiant heat",
      hvac_description_clean %in% c("Package Unit","Complete HVAC","Ventilation") ~ "Full HVAC or ventilation",
      hvac_description_clean %in% c("None","No Heat") ~ "No heating",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )
```

## 11.2 Improvement Detail Feature Extraction

The `detail_description` field contains specific characteristics of the improvements. By identifying key terms, new binary features are created to indicate the presence of certain amenities or property features.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    detail_description_clean = detail_description,
    has_bath_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Bath|Toilet|Shower|Sink|Fixture|Wet Bar|Laundry|Water Heater", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_garage_or_carport_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Garage|Carport", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_deck_or_porch_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Deck|Porch|Balcony|Entry|Open Slab|Concrete Slab", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_pool_or_spa_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Pool|Hot Tub|Spa|Sauna|Tennis", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_fireplace_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Fireplace|PreFab|Pre-Fab|Stove", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_storage_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Storage|Shed|Freezer|Cooler|Warehouse|Material|Equipment", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_waterfront_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Dock|Marina|Boat|Floats|Bulkhead|Pilings", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_parking_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Parking", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    has_finished_space_detail = str_detect(detail_description_clean, regex("Finished|Attic|Basement|Bsmnt|Office|Loft|Solar Room", ignore_case = TRUE))
  )

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    detail_group = case_when(
      has_bath_detail ~ "Plumbing or bath feature",
      has_garage_or_carport_detail ~ "Garage or carport",
      has_deck_or_porch_detail ~ "Outdoor living feature",
      has_pool_or_spa_detail ~ "Leisure amenity",
      has_fireplace_detail ~ "Fireplace or stove",
      has_storage_detail ~ "Storage feature",
      has_waterfront_detail ~ "Waterfront feature",
      has_parking_detail ~ "Parking feature",
      has_finished_space_detail ~ "Finished extra space",
      is.na(detail_description_clean) ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )
```

## 11.3 Use Description Grouping

The `use_description` field is grouped into broader categories. This creates a simplified `use_group` variable that helps distinguish residential, multi-unit housing, commercial, industrial, vacant land, public/community, and other use types.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    use_description_clean = str_trim(use_description),
    
    use_group = case_when(
      is.na(use_description_clean) ~ NA_character_,
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "SINGLE FAMILY|SFR|OTHER RESIDENTIAL|MOBILE|MFG HOME|MH TITLE|RM BOARDING HOUSE|RES INDIAN",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Residential",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "DUPLEX|TRIPLEX|FOURPLEX|MULTI FAM|APT|CONDO|SUBSIDIZED|RETIREMENT HOME|NURSING|GROUP QTRS|MH PARK",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Multi-unit housing",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "VACANT|VAC LND|VAC LAND|COMM VAC LAND|UNDEVELOPED|OTHER UNDEVEL|NOT A BLDG SITE|MAJOR PROBLEM|NO PERK",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Vacant land",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "RETAIL|STORE|MARKET|MART|RESTAURANT|FAST FOOD|TAVERN|BAR|HOTEL|MOTEL|CASINO|ESPRESSO|SALON|SPA|DISCOUNT|FURNISHINGS|APPAREL|FOOD RETAIL|SHOPPING|BIG BOX",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Commercial",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "OFFICE|BANK|CREDIT UNION|MEDICAL|DENTAL|VETERINARIAN|PROFESSIONAL|BUSINESS SERVICES|POSTAL|INSURANCE|REAL ESTATE|FINANCE",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Office and services",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "WAREHOUSE|STORAGE|MFG|MANUFACTURING|INDUSTRIAL|IND VAC|FAB METAL|LUMBER|WOOD MFG|FOOD MFG|CHEMICAL|PETRO|PAPER|PRINTING|MINING|QUARRY",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Industrial or storage",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "AUTO|CAR WASH|GAS STATION|FUELING|VEHICLE|RV SALES|USED CAR|MINI LUBE|REPAIR SERVICES",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Vehicle related",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "SCHOOL|UNIVERSITY|COLLEGE|EDUCATIONAL|RELIGIOUS|CHURCH|GOVERNMENT|FIRE STATION|PRISON|CEMETERIES|PUBLIC ASSEMBLY",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Public and community services",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "PARK|REC|GOLF|MARINA|BOAT|RESORT|CAMP|THEATER|CULTURAL|FISHING",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Leisure amenities",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "AGRI|FARM|FOREST|HORTICULTURAL|CULTIVATED|GREENBELT|OPEN SPACE|TIMBER|WETLAND",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Agriculture or open space",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "UTILITY|UTILITIES|WELL|WATER|DRAIN|COMMUNICATION|RIGHT OF WAY|TRANSPORT|TRANSIT|RAIL|AIRCRAFT|STREET",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Utility or transportation",
      
      str_detect(use_description_clean, regex(
        "MINERAL RIGHTS|TIDELANDS|WATER AREAS|TRANSFERRED DEVELOPMENT RIGHTS|FLOODWAY",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )) ~ "Land rights or special land",
      
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )
```

# 13. Categorical Redundancy Review Using Cramér's V

Cramér’s V is used to examine relationships between categorical variables.

This helps identify categorical features that may contain overlapping or redundant information. Highly related categorical variables are reviewed, and some are removed to reduce redundancy.

```{r}
# Select categorical columns
cramers_vars <- c(
  "deep_type",
  "improved_vacant",
  "appraisal_account_type_sale",
  "appraisal_account_type_appraisal",
  "utility_electric",
  "utility_sewer",
  "utility_water",
  "street_type",
  "property_type",
  "condition",
  "quality",
  "primary_occupancy_group",
  "hvac_group",
  "detail_group",
  "use_group",
  "account_type",
  "parent_child_indicator",
  "continued_indicator"
)

categorical_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(any_of(cramers_vars))

# Function to calculate Cramer's V safely
cramers_v <- function(x, y) {
  tbl <- table(x, y)
  
  if (nrow(tbl) < 2 || ncol(tbl) < 2) {
    return(NA)
  }
  
  cramerV(tbl)
}

# Create empty matrix
cat_vars <- names(categorical_df)

cramers_matrix <- matrix(
  NA,
  nrow = length(cat_vars),
  ncol = length(cat_vars),
  dimnames = list(cat_vars, cat_vars)
)

# Fill matrix
for (i in seq_along(cat_vars)) {
  for (j in seq_along(cat_vars)) {
    cramers_matrix[i, j] <- cramers_v(
      categorical_df[[cat_vars[i]]],
      categorical_df[[cat_vars[j]]]
    )
  }
}

# Plot heatmap
corrplot(
  cramers_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  tl.cex = 0.7,
  tl.col = "black",
  na.label = " "
)
```

Correlated categorical features are removed.

```{r}
cols_to_exclude <- c(
  # already used for filtering / not useful as model features
  "valid_invalid",
  "confirmed_unconfirmed",
  "exclude_reason",
  "improved_vacant",
  "appraisal_account_type_sale",
  "account_type",
  "deep_type",
  
  # duplicate / redundant appraisal type information
  "appraisal_account_type_sale",
  
  # parcel history/admin fields
  "parent_child_indicator",
  "continued_indicator",
  
  #other irrelevant columns
  "completed_date",
  
   # administrative/date information
  "appraisal_date",
  
  # raw detailed text columns replaced by grouped versions
  "primary_occupancy_description",
  "hvac_description",
  "detail_type",
  "detail_description",
  "use_description",
  
  # too detailed / may not add much for a general model
  "story_height",
  "interior",
  "roof_cover"
)

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-contains("clean"))

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-any_of(cols_to_exclude))
```

# 14. Numeric Redundancy Review Using Correlation Matrix

A numeric correlation matrix is used to examine relationships between numeric variables.

This helps identify numeric features that are highly correlated with each other or may create multicollinearity problems. Some redundant or administrative numeric fields are removed from the dataset.

```{r}
# Select only numeric columns
numeric_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(where(is.numeric))

# Create correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(
  numeric_df,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
)

# View correlation matrix
cor_matrix

# Plot heatmap
corrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  tl.cex = 0.7,
  tl.col = "black",
  na.label = " "
)
```

Redundant numeric features that are highly correlated with each other or with the target variable are removed to avoid multicollinearity issues in predictive modeling.

```{r}
numeric_cols_to_exclude <- c(
  # administrative / historical fields
  "parcel_count",
  "seg_merge_number",
  "tax_year",
  "tax_year_prior",
  "tax_year_current",
  
  # redundant year/age information

  "land_value_prior_year",
  "improvement_value_prior_year",
  "total_market_value_prior_year",
  "taxable_value_prior_year",
  "land_value_current_year",
  "improvement_value_current_year",
  "total_market_value_current_year",
  "taxable_value_current_year",
  
  # redundant land area fields - keep simpler parcel-level size fields
  "land_gross_acres",
  "land_gross_square_feet",
  "land_net_acres",
  "net_square_feet",
  "built_as_square_feet",
  
  "units_detail",
  "percent_complete",
  "built_as_length",
  "built_as_width",
  "land_width",
  "land_depth",
  "land_gross_front_feet",
  "sprinkler_square_feet",
  "year_remodeled"
)

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-any_of(numeric_cols_to_exclude))
```

# 15. Variance Check for Numeric Features

The remaining numeric features are reviewed using summary statistics, including missing values, unique values, minimum, maximum, mean, median, standard deviation, and variance.

This step helps identify variables with very low variation or unusual distributions that may not be useful for predictive modeling.

```{r}
numeric_summary <- joined_df %>%
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
  summarise(across(
    everything(),
    list(
      missing = ~ sum(is.na(.x)),
      unique_values = ~ n_distinct(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      min = ~ min(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      max = ~ max(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      median = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd = ~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      variance = ~ var(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
  )) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = c("column_name", ".value"),
    names_pattern = "(.+)_(missing|unique_values|min|max|mean|median|sd|variance)"
  ) %>%
  arrange(sd)

numeric_summary
```

# 16. Additional Feature Consolidation

Some related features are combined or updated to reduce redundancy and improve consistency.

For example, fireplace information is consolidated into one feature, and detail-based boolean indicators are updated using information from grouped detail categories and related numeric columns.

## 16.1 Fireplace Consolidation

Fireplace and `has_fireplace_detail` both indicate the presence of a fireplace. These features are combined into one fireplace indicator.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    has_fireplace_detail = case_when(
      fireplaces == 1 ~ TRUE,
      has_fireplace_detail == TRUE ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  ) %>%
  select(-any_of(c("fireplaces")))
```

```{r}
joined_df
```

## 16.2 Detail Feature Consolidation

Detail information is combined into grouped boolean features. This reduces the number of detailed text-based variables while keeping information about relevant property features.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    has_fireplace_detail = coalesce(has_fireplace_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Fireplace or stove", FALSE),
    has_garage_or_carport_detail = coalesce(has_garage_or_carport_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Garage or carport", FALSE),
    has_deck_or_porch_detail = coalesce(has_deck_or_porch_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Outdoor living feature", FALSE),
    has_pool_or_spa_detail = coalesce(has_pool_or_spa_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Leisure amenity", FALSE),
    has_storage_detail = coalesce(has_storage_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Storage feature", FALSE),
    has_waterfront_detail = coalesce(has_waterfront_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Waterfront feature", FALSE),
    has_parking_detail = coalesce(has_parking_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Parking feature", FALSE),
    has_finished_space_detail = coalesce(has_finished_space_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Finished extra space", FALSE),
    has_bath_detail = coalesce(has_bath_detail, FALSE) | coalesce(detail_group == "Plumbing or bath feature", FALSE)
  )
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-any_of("detail_group"))
```

# 17. Redundancy Checks

Potentially overlapping features are compared before removal.

This ensures that columns are not removed without first checking whether they provide additional useful information.

## 17.1 Bathroom Detail Check

Bathroom detail information is compared with the numeric bathroom count.

```{r}
joined_df %>%
  group_by(has_bath_detail) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    avg_bathrooms = mean(bathrooms, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bathrooms = median(bathrooms, na.rm = TRUE),
    missing_bathrooms = sum(is.na(bathrooms)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    has_bath_detail = case_when(
      has_bath_detail == TRUE ~ TRUE,
      has_bath_detail == FALSE & !is.na(bathrooms) & bathrooms > 0 ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )
```

Deck or porch detail information is compared with porch square footage.

```{r}
    avg_porch_sqft = mean(porch_square_feet, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_porch_sqft = median(porch_square_feet, na.rm = TRUE),
    missing_porch_sqft = sum(is.na(porch_square_feet)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    has_deck_or_porch_detail = case_when(
      has_deck_or_porch_detail == TRUE ~ TRUE,
      has_deck_or_porch_detail == FALSE & !is.na(porch_square_feet) & porch_square_feet > 0 ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )
```

## 17.3 Garage or Carport Detail Check

Garage or carport detail information is compared with attached garage square footage.

```{r}
joined_df %>%
  group_by(has_garage_or_carport_detail) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    avg_attached_garage_sqft = mean(attached_garage_square_feet, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_attached_garage_sqft = median(attached_garage_square_feet, na.rm = TRUE),
    missing_attached_garage_sqft = sum(is.na(attached_garage_square_feet)),
    .groups = "drop"

```

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    has_garage_or_carport_detail = case_when(
      has_garage_or_carport_detail == TRUE ~ TRUE,
      has_garage_or_carport_detail == FALSE & !is.na(attached_garage_square_feet) & attached_garage_square_feet > 0 ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )
```

## 17.4 Property Classification Overlap Check

Property classification variables are compared with each other to identify redundant information.

```{r}
joined_df %>%
  count(appraisal_account_type_appraisal, property_type, use_group, sort = TRUE)

joined_df %>%
  distinct(appraisal_account_type_appraisal, property_type, use_group) %>%
  arrange(appraisal_account_type_appraisal, property_type, use_group)
```

The variables `appraisal_account_type_appraisal`, `property_type`, and `use_group` describe similar aspects of property classification. Since `use_group` provides a simplified and more interpretable version of property use, and `property_type` describes the building/improvement type, `appraisal_account_type_appraisal` was removed to reduce redundancy.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-any_of("appraisal_account_type_appraisal"))
```

## 17.5 Sale Price Comparison for Detail Features

The selected boolean features are compared against median sale price to evaluate whether they may still provide useful price-related information.

```{r}
joined_df %>%
  group_by(has_bath_detail) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

joined_df %>%
  group_by(has_deck_or_porch_detail) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"

joined_df %>%
  group_by(has_garage_or_carport_detail) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

joined_df %>%
  group_by(has_parking_detail) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Based on the comparison, `has_bath_detail` is removed because the numeric `bathrooms` column already provides more direct information.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-any_of("has_bath_detail"))
```

# 19. Data Dictionary for Prepared Dataset

The data dictionary explains the final variables included in the analysis dataset.

For each variable, the dictionary provides the variable name, a description, and the reason why the variable is useful for the analysis.

| Variable | Description | Why it is useful |
|-------------------|----------------------------------|-------------------|
| `sale_date` | Date when the property sale was recorded or legally sold. | Helps capture market changes over time, such as price trends by year or period. |
| `sale_price` | Recorded sale price of the property. This is the target variable for price prediction. | This is the value the model will try to predict. |
| `buildings` | Number of buildings or improvements located on the parcel. | More buildings or improvements can affect property value. |
| `land_net_square_feet` | Size of the individual parcel in square feet. | Land size is often an important factor in property value. |
| `utility_electric` | Indicates whether electric power is installed, available, or not available for the property. | Utility access can influence usability and value. |
| `utility_sewer` | Indicates whether sewer or septic service is installed, available, or not available. | Sewer or septic availability can affect development potential and property value. |
| `utility_water` | Indicates whether water service is installed, available, or not available. | Water access is essential for property use and can affect value. |
| `street_type` | Describes the type of road access to the property, such as paved road, unpaved road, or no road access. | Road access can influence accessibility, desirability, and value. |
| `latitude` | Latitude coordinate of the parcel location. | Captures geographic location, which is highly relevant for property prices. |
| `longitude` | Longitude coordinate of the parcel location. | Captures geographic location, which is highly relevant for property prices. |
| `property_type` | Classification of the building or improvement type, such as residential, commercial, mobile home, or other property types. | Helps distinguish different types of structures that may follow different price patterns. |
| `neighborhood` | Assessor neighborhood code representing an area with similar location and market characteristics. | Location and neighborhood are usually strong drivers of property price. |
| `square_feet` | Total building square footage recorded for the property improvement. | Building size is one of the most important predictors of property value. |
| `condition` | Overall condition of the structure, reflecting maintenance, upkeep, and depreciation. | Better condition can increase value, while poor condition can reduce value. |
| `quality` | Quality rating of the structure, reflecting materials, workmanship, design, and construction quality. | Higher construction quality is usually associated with higher property value. |
| `porch_square_feet` | Total square footage of porch areas associated with the property. | Additional outdoor living space may increase property appeal and value. |
| `attached_garage_square_feet` | Total square footage of attached or built-in garage space. | Garage space can increase convenience, storage, and overall property value. |
| `exterior` | Predominant exterior material or siding used on the building. | Exterior material can reflect construction quality, maintenance needs, and market appeal. |
| `stories` | Number of floors or building levels above grade, excluding attic and basement areas. | Building layout and number of levels can influence usable space and buyer preference. |
| `bedrooms` | Number of bedrooms listed for the residential property. | Bedroom count is a common and important housing characteristic for buyers. |
| `bathrooms` | Number of bathrooms listed for the residential property, often represented as a decimal. | Bathroom count strongly affects comfort, functionality, and property value. |
| `units` | Number of separate units within the building. | Helps distinguish single-unit from multi-unit properties, which can have different values. |
| `year_built` | Year the building was originally constructed. | Property age can affect value, maintenance needs, and building standards. |
| `primary_occupancy_group` | Simplified category describing the main occupancy or use of the building. | Helps group properties by broad use type, making patterns easier to analyze. |
| `hvac_group` | Simplified category describing the heating, ventilation, or HVAC system type. | Heating and HVAC systems can affect comfort, energy efficiency, and value. |
| `has_garage_or_carport_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether garage or carport-related detail was recorded. | Captures additional parking or covered vehicle storage features. |
| `has_deck_or_porch_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether deck, porch, balcony, or outdoor living detail was recorded. | Outdoor living features can improve property appeal. |
| `has_pool_or_spa_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether pool, hot tub, spa, sauna, tennis, or similar leisure amenity detail was recorded. | Leisure amenities can add value for some properties. |
| `has_fireplace_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether fireplace or stove-related detail was recorded. | Fireplaces or stoves can increase comfort and market appeal. |
| `has_storage_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether storage-related detail was recorded. | Extra storage can improve functionality and usability. |
| `has_waterfront_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether dock, marina, boat, float, bulkhead, piling, or other waterfront-related detail was recorded. | Waterfront-related features can strongly influence property value. |
| `has_parking_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether parking-related detail was recorded. | Parking availability can affect convenience and property desirability. |
| `has_finished_space_detail` | Boolean indicator showing whether finished attic, basement, office, loft, solar room, or other finished extra space was recorded. | Finished extra space can increase usable area and value. |
| `use_group` | Simplified category describing the overall property use, such as residential, multi-unit housing, commercial, industrial, vacant land, public/community service, or other use types. | Helps separate properties with different use types and price behavior. |

# 20. Transition to Exploratory Data Analysis

After the data preparation and feature selection steps, the next phase is exploratory data analysis.

The EDA will focus on understanding:

-   The distribution of sale prices
-   Price trends over time
-   Relationships between numeric features and sale price
-   Differences in sale price across categorical groups
-   Outliers and unusual values
-   Missing values in the final dataset
-   Which features appear most relevant for house price prediction

# 21. Exploratory Data Analysis

The exploratory data analysis focuses on understanding the final prepared dataset before modeling. The main goal is to analyze the distribution of the target variable, investigate relationships between features and sale price, identify outliers, and understand which variables may be most relevant for price prediction.

## 21.1 Target Variable Analysis: Sale Price

The target variable for this project is `sale_price`. Before analyzing the relationship between house prices and other features, the distribution of sale prices is examined. This helps identify skewness, extreme values, and unusual transactions that may affect later modeling.

```{r}
summary(joined_df$sale_price)
```

The sale price distribution is strongly right-skewed. The median sale price is 303,000 USD, while the mean sale price is higher at 581,189 USD, indicating that very expensive properties are pulling the average upward. The minimum sale price is 1 USD, which is likely not a normal market transaction, and the maximum sale price is 198,274,450 USD, which is an extreme outlier. Therefore, sale price outliers should be investigated before modeling.

```{r}
joined_df %>%
  summarise(
    sales_below_10000 = sum(sale_price < 10000, na.rm = TRUE),
    sales_below_50000 = sum(sale_price < 50000, na.rm = TRUE),
    sales_above_1000000 = sum(sale_price > 1000000, na.rm = TRUE),
    sales_above_5000000 = sum(sale_price > 5000000, na.rm = TRUE),
    sales_above_10000000 = sum(sale_price > 10000000, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

The outlier check shows that there are 1,954 sales below 10,000 USD and 10,458 sales below 50,000 USD. These very low sale prices may represent unusual transactions, partial sales, mobile homes, land-only sales, or records that do not reflect typical house market prices.

On the upper end, there are 19,138 sales above 1,000,000 USD, 2,900 sales above 5,000,000 USD, and 1,639 sales above 10,000,000 USD. These high-value sales may represent luxury properties, commercial properties, multi-parcel transactions, or other non-standard residential sales. Therefore, the sale price distribution should be investigated further before deciding whether to filter outliers or keep them.

### 21.1.1 Outliers lower than 10,000 USD

```{r}
# Very low sale prices
joined_df %>%
  filter(sale_price < 10000) %>%
  select(sale_price, sale_date, property_type, use_group, square_feet, land_net_square_feet) %>%
  arrange(sale_price) %>%
  head(10)
```

As a first outlier-cleaning step, records with sale prices below 10,000 USD were removed. The inspection of low-price records showed that many of these transactions had extremely small sale prices, such as 1 USD, 50 USD, or 100 USD, which are unlikely to represent normal market transactions.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  filter(sale_price >= 10000)
```

### 21.1.2 Outliers higher than 10,000,000 USD

```{r}
# Very high sale prices
joined_df %>%
  filter(sale_price > 10000000) %>%
  select(sale_price, sale_date, property_type, use_group, square_feet, land_net_square_feet) %>%
  arrange(desc(sale_price)) %>%
  head(20)
```

The inspection of the highest sale prices shows that the most expensive records are mainly industrial, commercial, or multi-unit properties. These properties have very large building areas and land sizes, such as industrial properties with more than 1,000,000 square feet of building area. Therefore, these extreme high-value records do not represent typical residential house sales and should be treated separately.

For our analysis only residential properties will be included, so these high-value commercial and industrial sales will be removed.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  filter(
    property_type == "Residential",
    use_group == "Residential"
  )
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  distinct()

nrow(joined_df)
summary(joined_df$sale_price)
```

After filtering the dataset to residential properties and removing records with sale prices below 10,000 USD, the dataset contains 254,567 records. The sale price distribution is still right-skewed, but it is more representative of residential house sales. The median sale price is 320,000 USD, while the mean sale price is 397,055 USD, indicating that higher-priced residential properties still pull the average upward. The maximum sale price is 8,500,000 USD, which may represent luxury residential properties and should be reviewed further.

### 21.1.3 Additional Feature Reduction

The utility variables and and other variables are removed because they are highly imbalanced after filtering to residential properties. Almost all residential properties have electric, sewer/septic, and water access, so these columns add little variation for the remaining analysis.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(
    -any_of(c(
      "utility_electric",
      "utility_sewer",
      "utility_water",
      "street_type",
      "condition",
      "property_type", 
      "use_group",
      "has_fireplace_detail",
      "has_parking_detail"
    ))
  )

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  distinct()
```

### 21.1.4 Target Variable Analysis: Sale Price Distribution

```{r}
p1 <- ggplot(joined_df, aes(x = sale_price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of \nSale Price",
    x = "Sale Price in USD",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  )

p2 <- ggplot(joined_df, aes(x = sale_price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of \nSale Price on \nLog Scale",
    x = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  )

p3 <- ggplot(joined_df, aes(y = sale_price)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Sale Price Outliers",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale"
  )

p1 + p2 + p3 + plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

The histogram confirms that sale prices are right-skewed, meaning that most properties are concentrated in the lower and middle price ranges, while a smaller number of properties have very high sale prices. The log-scale histogram makes the distribution easier to interpret by reducing the visual impact of extreme high values. The boxplot also confirms the presence of high-value outliers, which is expected in property price data.

## 21.2 Sale Price Over Time

After analyzing the overall distribution of sale prices, the next step is to examine how sale prices changed over time. Since the dataset contains a `sale_date` variable, prices can be summarized by year to identify market trends and changes in typical sale prices.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    sale_year = year(sale_date)
  )

sale_price_by_year <- joined_df %>%
  group_by(sale_year) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_sale_price = mean(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(sale_price_by_year, aes(x = sale_year, y = median_sale_price)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Sale Price Over Time",
    x = "Sale Year",
    y = "Median Sale Price in USD"
  )
```

This analysis shows how the typical sale price changed across years. The median sale price is used because it is less affected by extreme values than the mean sale price.

The median sale price shows a clear upward trend over time. Prices increased gradually from the late 1990s to the mid-2000s, followed by a decline around the 2008–2010 period. After that, median sale prices started increasing again, with a stronger rise after approximately 2015. The strongest growth appears in the most recent years, where the median sale price reaches its highest levels. This suggests that `sale_date` or a derived time variable such as `sale_year` may be important for the price prediction model.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    sale_year = lubridate::year(sale_date) # keeping it as a feature since it shows a clear relationship with sale price
  )
```

## 21.3 Bivariate Analysis

In this section, the relationship between `sale_price` and the remaining features is explored. The goal is to understand which variables may have a visible relationship with property prices and may therefore be useful for later modeling.

The analysis is split into numeric, categorical, boolean, location, and time-based features.

```{r}
numeric_features <- c(
  "buildings",
  "land_net_square_feet",
  "latitude",
  "longitude",
  "square_feet",
  "porch_square_feet",
  "attached_garage_square_feet",
  "stories",
  "bedrooms",
  "bathrooms",
  "units",
  "year_built",
  "sale_year"
)

categorical_features <- c(
  "neighborhood",
  "quality",
  "exterior",
  "primary_occupancy_group",
  "hvac_group"
)

boolean_features <- c(
  "has_garage_or_carport_detail",
  "has_deck_or_porch_detail",
  "has_pool_or_spa_detail",
  "has_storage_detail",
  "has_waterfront_detail",
  "has_finished_space_detail"
)

categorical_features <- categorical_features[categorical_features %in% names(joined_df)]
boolean_features <- boolean_features[boolean_features %in% names(joined_df)]
```

### 21.3.1 Numeric Feature Correlation with Sale Price

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=5}
# Correlation table
numeric_correlations <- joined_df %>%
  select(sale_price, all_of(numeric_features)) %>%
  summarise(across(
    all_of(numeric_features),
    ~ cor(.x, sale_price, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  )) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "feature",
    values_to = "correlation"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    correlation = round(correlation, 3)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(correlation)))

# Plot
correlation_plot <- ggplot(numeric_correlations, aes(
  x = reorder(feature, correlation),
  y = correlation
)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Between Numeric Features and Sale Price",
    x = "Numeric Feature",
    y = "Correlation with Sale Price"
  )

# Table
correlation_table <- tableGrob(
  numeric_correlations,
  rows = NULL
)

# Show plot and table side by side
correlation_plot + wrap_elements(correlation_table) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1))
```

The correlation results show that `sale_year` has the strongest positive correlation with `sale_price`, suggesting that prices increased over time. Building size, represented by `square_feet`, also has a clear positive relationship with sale price. Other property characteristics such as `bathrooms`, `porch_square_feet`, `attached_garage_square_feet`, and `bedrooms` also show positive correlations, meaning that larger or better-equipped homes tend to have higher sale prices.

The correlations are moderate rather than extremely high, which means that no single numeric feature fully explains sale price on its own. This suggests that house prices are influenced by a combination of time, size, location, and property characteristics.

The numeric bivariate plots show that several property characteristics have a visible relationship with sale price. Building size has a positive relationship with sale price: as `square_feet` increases, sale prices generally tend to increase as well, although there is still a lot of variation. The bathroom and bedroom plots show that properties with more bathrooms and bedrooms generally have higher sale prices. However, the relationship is not perfectly linear, and there are some extreme values, especially for properties with unusually high numbers of bedrooms or bathrooms. The year-built plot suggests that newer properties tend to have somewhat higher sale prices, but the relationship is weaker and more scattered than for building size. This indicates that age alone does not explain sale price, but it may still provide useful information together with other features.

The additional numeric bivariate plots show that land size, porch area, garage area, and number of buildings also have relationships with sale price. `land_net_square_feet` shows a positive but scattered relationship with sale price. Larger land parcels tend to have higher prices, but the relationship is not very strong on its own. This suggests that land size matters, but location and building characteristics likely explain much of the remaining variation. `porch_square_feet` also shows a positive relationship with sale price. | Importance level | Numeric features | Reason |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|

| **Important** | `bathrooms`, `bedrooms` | More bathrooms and bedrooms were generally associated with higher sale prices. |
| **Important** | `land_net_square_feet` | Larger land parcels tended to have higher prices, although the relationship was scattered. |
| **Moderately important** | `porch_square_feet`, `attached_garage_square_feet` | Outdoor space and garage space were associated with higher sale prices. |
| **Moderately important** | `year_built` | Newer homes tended to have somewhat higher prices, but the relationship was weaker and more scattered. |
| **Less important / weaker** | `buildings`, `stories`, `units`, `latitude`, `longitude` | These may still be useful, but their individual numeric relationships with sale price were weaker or harder to interpret directly. |

## 21.4 Categorical Features vs Sale Price

After analyzing numeric features, categorical variables are analyzed to understand how sale prices differ across different property groups. Since sale prices are skewed and contain high-value outliers, the median sale price is used instead of the mean because it is less affected by extreme values.

```{r}
plot_categorical_vs_price <- function(df, column_name) {
  df %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[column_name]])) %>%
    group_by(.data[[column_name]]) %>%
    summarise(
      count = n(),
      median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(median_sale_price)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(
      x = reorder(.data[[column_name]], median_sale_price),
      y = median_sale_price
    )) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      title = paste("Median Sale Price by", column_name),
      x = column_name,
      y = "Median Sale Price in USD"
    )
}
```

### 21.4.1 Main categorical features

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}

p2
```

### 21.4.6 Categorical Feature Summary

The categorical bivariate analysis shows that several categorical variables are related to differences in median sale price.

The `quality` variable shows the clearest and most meaningful pattern. Properties with higher quality ratings generally have higher median sale prices. For example, properties rated `Excellent`, `Very Good Plus`, and `Very Good` have much higher median sale prices than properties rated `Average`, `Fair`, or `Low`. This suggests that construction quality is an important factor in explaining property value.

The `condition` variable is less straightforward. Most properties are classified as `Average`, while the other condition categories contain much fewer observations. Some smaller categories, such as `Poor` or `Very Poor`, do not follow a fully intuitive price pattern. Therefore, condition should be interpreted carefully, especially for categories with low counts.

The utility variables show that properties with electric power, sewer/septic, and water available or installed generally have higher median sale prices than properties without these utilities. However, the groups without utilities contain very few observations, this is why these variables will not be considered for the further analysis.

The `street_type` variable shows only a small difference between properties with road access and properties with limited or no road access. This suggests that street access may be less important in the filtered residential dataset, or that most properties already have adequate road access, this is why it is removed.

The `exterior` and `hvac_group` variables show visible differences in median sale price across categories. Some exterior types and heating systems are associated with higher median prices, but several categories have low counts. These differences may also reflect other factors, such as location, property quality, or property age.

The `property_type` and `use_group` variables only contain residential values after filtering the dataset. Therefore, they no longer explain differences in sale price within the current residential analysis dataset.

The `neighborhood` variable shows strong differences in median sale price across neighborhood codes. This confirms that location is an important factor in property prices. However, some neighborhood categories have very few observations, so low-count neighborhoods should be handled carefully in later modeling.

Overall, the categorical analysis suggests that `quality`, `neighborhood`, `hvac_group`, `exterior`, and utility availability may be useful categorical predictors. At the same time, category counts must be considered because small groups can produce unstable median sale prices.

| Importance level | Features | Summary |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Most important** | `quality`, `neighborhood` | These variables showed the clearest relationship with median sale price. Quality captures construction level, while neighborhood captures location differences. |
| **Moderately important** | `exterior`, `hvac_group` | These variables showed visible price differences across categories, but some categories had low counts and may also reflect other factors such as quality, age, or location. |
| **Weak / uncertain / removed** | `condition` | The pattern was less intuitive and several categories had low counts, so this variable should be interpreted carefully or removed. |
| **Least important / removed** | `utility_electric`, `utility_sewer`, `utility_water`, `street_type`, `property_type`, `use_group` | These variables were either highly imbalanced, showed only small price differences, or contained only residential values after filtering. |

## 21.5 Boolean Features vs Sale Price

The boolean features indicate whether specific property details or amenities are present. These variables are analyzed by comparing median sale prices for properties where the feature is present versus not present.

```{r}
boolean_price_summary <- bind_rows(
  lapply(boolean_features, function(feature) {
    joined_df %>%
      group_by(.data[[feature]]) %>%
      summarise(
        count = n(),
        median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
        mean_sale_price = mean(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      ) %>%
      mutate(feature = feature) %>%
      rename(value = .data[[feature]])
  })
)

boolean_price_summary

ggplot(boolean_price_summary, aes(
  x = feature,
  y = median_sale_price,
  fill = value
)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Sale Price by Boolean Property Features",
    x = "Feature",
    y = "Median Sale Price in USD",
    fill = "Feature Present"
  )
```

```{r}
boolean_feature_counts <- bind_rows(
  lapply(boolean_features, function(feature) {
    joined_df %>%
      count(.data[[feature]]) %>%
      mutate(feature = feature) %>%
      rename(value = .data[[feature]])
  })
)

boolean_feature_counts
```

The boolean feature count summary shows that most engineered features have both `TRUE` and `FALSE` values and can therefore provide useful variation for analysis. Garage/carport, deck/porch, fireplace, storage, waterfront, pool/spa, and finished-space indicators all contain both categories.

However, some features are highly imbalanced. For example, `has_pool_or_spa_detail` is `TRUE` for only 3,272 records, and `has_waterfront_detail` is `TRUE` for only 2,067 records. These features may still be important because they are associated with higher median sale prices, but their small counts should be considered during modeling.

```{r}
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(-any_of("has_parking_detail"))
```

## 21.5.1 Boolean Features Summary

| Importance level | Features | Summary |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Most important** | `has_waterfront_detail`, `has_finished_space_detail` | These features showed clear differences in median sale price. Waterfront details were associated with much higher prices, while finished extra space added value across different home sizes. |
| **Important** | `has_pool_or_spa_detail`, `has_garage_or_carport_detail`, `has_deck_or_porch_detail` | These features were generally associated with higher median sale prices. Pool/spa features were rare but potentially valuable, while garage/carport and deck/porch details represented useful property amenities. |
| **Moderately important** | `has_storage_detail` | Storage details showed some price differences and may add useful information, but the relationship was weaker than waterfront, finished space, garage, or pool/spa features. |
| **Weak / uncertain** | `has_fireplace_detail` | This feature did not show a strong positive pattern. It may not capture fireplace value consistently or may be related to older properties. This feature was removed. |
| **Least important / removed** | `has_parking_detail` | This feature had no `TRUE` values after filtering to residential properties, so it provided no useful variation and was removed. This feature was removed. |

## 21.6 Missing Values in the Final Dataset

After completing the bivariate analysis, missing values are checked again in the final prepared dataset. This step helps identify which variables need imputation, replacement, or removal before modeling.

```{r}
missing_final <- data.frame(
  column_name = names(joined_df),
  missing_count = sapply(joined_df, function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  missing_percent = round(sapply(joined_df, function(x) mean(is.na(x))) * 100, 2),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing_percent))

missing_final %>%
  filter(missing_count > 0)

```

```{r}
# Replace with 0
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  mutate(
    attached_garage_square_feet = case_when(
      is.na(attached_garage_square_feet) & has_garage_or_carport_detail == FALSE ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ attached_garage_square_feet
    ),
    porch_square_feet = case_when(
      is.na(porch_square_feet) & coalesce(has_deck_or_porch_detail, FALSE) == FALSE ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ porch_square_feet
    )
  )

# Remove missing values
joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(attached_garage_square_feet),
    !is.na(porch_square_feet),
    !is.na(land_net_square_feet),
    !is.na(latitude),
    !is.na(longitude),
    !is.na(bedrooms),
    !is.na(bathrooms),
    !is.na(units)
  )
```

## 21.7 Key Findings from the Bivariate Analysis

The following table summarizes the key findings from the exploratory data analysis regarding the relationships between features and sale price. This summary can help guide feature selection and engineering for the later modeling phase.

| Importance area | Feature(s) | What the EDA showed | Interpretation |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Time | `sale_year` | Sale year showed the strongest numeric relationship with `sale_price`. Median sale prices increased clearly over time. | Market timing is important because house prices changed substantially across years. |
| Building size | `square_feet` | Larger homes generally had higher sale prices. | Building size is one of the most important property characteristics. |
| Location | `neighborhood`, `latitude`, `longitude` | Median sale prices differed strongly across neighborhood codes. Latitude and longitude capture geographic location. | Location is a major driver of property value. |
| Construction quality | `quality` | Higher quality ratings were associated with higher median sale prices. | Better construction quality generally increases property value. |
| Rooms | `bathrooms`, `bedrooms` | Properties with more bathrooms and bedrooms generally had higher sale prices. | Room count reflects property size, comfort, and functionality. |
| Land size | `land_net_square_feet` | Larger land parcels tended to have higher prices, but the relationship was scattered. | Land size matters, but it does not explain price on its own. |
| Garage and outdoor space | `attached_garage_square_feet`, `porch_square_feet`, `has_garage_or_carport_detail`, `has_deck_or_porch_detail` | Garage space and porch/deck features were associated with higher median sale prices. | Parking and outdoor living space can increase property appeal and value. |
| Amenities | `has_waterfront_detail`, `has_pool_or_spa_detail`, `has_finished_space_detail`, `has_storage_detail` | Waterfront and pool/spa features showed higher median prices, but they were rare. Finished space and storage also showed price differences. | Special amenities may add value, but rare features should be interpreted carefully. |
| Utilities | `utility_electric`, `utility_sewer`, `utility_water` | Properties without utilities had lower median sale prices, but these categories had very small counts. | Utility access may affect value, but the small “no utility” groups should be treated with caution. |

## 21.8 Interaction Analysis

After analyzing individual variables, selected interactions between important features are explored. Interaction analysis helps show whether the relationship between a feature and `sale_price` changes depending on another feature.

### 21.8.1 Square Feet × Quality

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
quality_order <- c(
  "Low",
  "Low Plus",
  "Fair",
  "Fair Plus",
  "Average",
  "Average Plus",
  "Good",
  "Good Plus",
  "Very Good",
  "Very Good Plus",
  "Excellent"
)

# Raw interaction plot
p_raw <- ggplot(
  joined_df %>%
    filter(
      !is.na(square_feet),
      !is.na(sale_price),
      !is.na(quality),
      sale_price > 0
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      quality = factor(quality, levels = quality_order, ordered = TRUE)
    ),
  aes(x = square_feet, y = sale_price, color = quality)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Raw Interaction Between Building Size and Quality",
    x = "Building Square Feet",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale",
    color = "Quality"
  )

# Aggregated median plot
p_aggregated <- joined_df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(square_feet),
    !is.na(quality),
    !is.na(sale_price)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    quality = factor(quality, levels = quality_order, ordered = TRUE),
    square_feet_group = cut(
      square_feet,
      breaks = quantile(square_feet, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25), na.rm = TRUE),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(square_feet_group, quality) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(count >= 30) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = square_feet_group, y = median_sale_price, fill = quality)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Aggregated Median Sale Price by Building Size Group and Quality",
    x = "Building Square Feet Group",
    y = "Median Sale Price in USD",
    fill = "Quality"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

p_raw / p_aggregated +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1.2, 1))
```

The interaction plot between building size and quality shows that sale prices generally increase with larger building size. At the same time, higher quality categories tend to appear more often in the upper price range. This suggests that both building size and construction quality are important for sale price, and that larger homes with higher quality ratings tend to sell for higher prices.

### 21.8.2 Bathrooms × Quality

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
joined_df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(bathrooms),
    !is.na(quality),
    !is.na(sale_price)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    quality = factor(quality, levels = quality_order, ordered = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  group_by(bathrooms, quality) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(count >= 30) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bathrooms, y = median_sale_price, color = quality)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Interaction Between Bathrooms and Quality",
    x = "Bathrooms",
    y = "Median Sale Price in USD",
    color = "Quality"
  )
```

The interaction between bathrooms and quality shows that median sale price generally increases as the number of bathrooms increases. This pattern is especially visible for higher-quality homes. Properties with higher quality ratings, such as `Very Good`, `Very Good Plus`, and `Excellent`, tend to have higher median sale prices at similar bathroom counts compared with lower-quality properties.

The lines also show that the effect of bathrooms is not the same for every quality level. For higher-quality homes, additional bathrooms are associated with much higher median sale prices, while for lower-quality homes the increase is more moderate. This suggests that bathrooms and quality interact: the value of additional bathrooms appears stronger when the overall construction quality is higher.

Some fluctuations at higher bathroom counts should be interpreted carefully because there may be fewer observations in those groups.

### 21.8.3 Square Feet × Sale Year

This checks whether the value of larger homes changes over time.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
joined_df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(square_feet),
    !is.na(sale_year),
    !is.na(sale_price)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    square_feet_group = cut(
      square_feet,
      breaks = quantile(square_feet, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25), na.rm = TRUE),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(sale_year, square_feet_group) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(count >= 30) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sale_year, y = median_sale_price, color = square_feet_group)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Sale Price Over Time by Building Size Group",
    x = "Sale Year",
    y = "Median Sale Price in USD",
    color = "Square Feet Group"
  )
```

The interaction between sale year and building size shows that median sale prices increased over time for all building-size groups. Larger homes consistently have higher median sale prices than smaller homes across the full time period.

The price gap between smaller and larger homes also appears to become wider in more recent years. This suggests that building size and time interact: larger homes did not only remain more expensive, but their prices increased more strongly over time compared with smaller homes.

The plot also shows a visible decline around the 2008–2010 period, followed by a recovery and stronger price growth after approximately 2015. This pattern is consistent across all building-size groups, but the increase is strongest for the largest homes.

### 21.8.4 Neighborhood × Sale Year

This checks whether price trends differ by neighborhood. Since there may be many neighborhoods, this uses the top 10 by number of records.

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
top_neighborhoods <- joined_df %>%
  count(neighborhood, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  pull(neighborhood)

joined_df %>%
  filter(
    neighborhood %in% top_neighborhoods,
    !is.na(sale_year),
    !is.na(sale_price)
  ) %>%
  group_by(sale_year, neighborhood) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(count >= 20) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sale_year, y = median_sale_price, color = as.factor(neighborhood))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Sale Price Over Time by Top Neighborhoods",
    x = "Sale Year",
    y = "Median Sale Price in USD",
    color = "Neighborhood"
  )
```

The interaction between neighborhood and sale year shows that median sale prices increased over time in all top neighborhoods, but the price levels and growth rates differ across neighborhoods. Some neighborhoods consistently have higher median sale prices than others, indicating that location is a key factor in property value.
