### 21.8.9 Summary of Interaction Analysis

| Interaction | Main finding | Interpretation |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `sale_year` × `neighborhood` | Median sale prices increased over time across the top neighborhoods, but growth patterns differed by neighborhood. | Time and location interact. Some neighborhoods experienced stronger price growth than others. |
| `square_feet` × `quality` | Larger homes generally had higher sale prices, especially when they also had higher quality ratings. | Building size and construction quality reinforce each other. Large, high-quality homes tend to achieve the highest prices. |
| `bathrooms` × `quality` | More bathrooms were associated with higher median sale prices, especially in higher-quality homes. | The value of additional bathrooms depends partly on the overall quality of the property. |
| `square_feet` × `has_finished_space_detail` | Properties with finished extra space had higher median sale prices across all building-size groups. | Finished extra space appears to add value beyond the main building square footage. |
| `quality` × `has_pool_or_spa_detail` | Pool or spa details were associated with higher median sale prices in several quality groups, especially higher-quality homes. | Pool/spa amenities may add value, but the feature is relatively rare and should be interpreted carefully. |
| `land_net_square_feet` × `has_waterfront_detail` | Waterfront properties were rare, but appeared in higher price ranges. | Waterfront details may add value, especially when combined with land characteristics, but the small number of observations requires caution. |
| `square_feet` × `has_garage_or_carport_detail` | Properties without garage/carport detail sometimes had slightly higher median sale prices within building-size groups. | This result is less intuitive and may reflect missing detail records, location effects, or that the indicator does not fully capture garage value. |

Overall, the interaction analysis shows that the relationships between features and sale price are complex and often depend on other factors. Building size, construction quality, location, amenities, and time all interact in ways that influence property values. These interactions suggest that a multivariate modeling approach will be necessary to capture the combined effects of these features on sale price.

## 21.9 EDA Conclusion

The exploratory data analysis showed that \`sale_price\` is influenced by a combination of time, location, building characteristics, property quality, and selected amenities.

The target variable \`sale_price\` was strongly right-skewed, with a small number of very high-value properties pulling the mean above the median. Very low sale prices below 10,000 USD were removed because they were unlikely to represent normal market transactions. The dataset was also filtered to residential properties, which made the sale price distribution more representative for the goal of predicting house prices.\
\
The time-based analysis showed that sale prices increased clearly over the years. The variable \`sale_year\` had the strongest numeric relationship with \`sale_price\`, indicating that market trends over time are an important factor in explaining property value.\
\
The numeric bivariate analysis showed that \`square_feet\`, \`bathrooms\`, \`bedrooms\`, \`land_net_square_feet\`, \`porch_square_feet\`, \`attached_garage_square_feet\`, and \`year_built\` are relevant numeric predictors. Larger homes, properties with more rooms, larger land parcels, garage space, and outdoor areas generally had higher sale prices.\
\
The categorical analysis showed that \`quality\` and \`neighborhood\` were the most important categorical variables. Higher quality ratings were associated with higher median sale prices, and median prices differed strongly across neighborhood codes. This confirms that both construction quality and location play an important role in property value. \`exterior\` and \`hvac_group\` also showed some useful differences, while variables such as utilities, street type, property type, and use group were removed because they were either highly imbalanced or no longer meaningful after filtering to residential properties.\
\
The boolean feature analysis showed that selected amenities may also contribute to property value. \`has_waterfront_detail\`, \`has_finished_space_detail\`, \`has_pool_or_spa_detail\`, \`has_garage_or_carport_detail\`, and \`has_deck_or_porch_detail\` showed meaningful differences in median sale price. However, rare features such as waterfront and pool/spa details should be interpreted carefully because they contain relatively few observations.\
\
The interaction analysis confirmed that sale price is not explained by single variables alone. Important interactions were observed between \`sale_year\` and \`neighborhood\`, \`square_feet\` and \`quality\`, \`bathrooms\` and \`quality\`, and \`square_feet\` with finished extra space. These findings suggest that the final model should be able to capture non-linear relationships and interactions between time, location, size, quality, and amenities.

| Feature | Why it is important |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `sale_year` | Captures market price changes over time. Sale prices increased clearly across years. |
| `neighborhood` | Captures location differences, which strongly affect property prices. |
| `latitude`, `longitude` | Provide precise geographic coordinates and help capture location patterns within and across neighborhoods. |
| `square_feet` | Represents building size. Larger homes generally had higher sale prices. |
| `quality` | Captures construction quality. Higher quality ratings were associated with higher median prices. |
| `bathrooms` | More bathrooms were generally associated with higher sale prices. |
| `bedrooms` | More bedrooms were generally associated with higher sale prices. |
| `land_net_square_feet` | Represents land size. Larger parcels tended to have higher prices. |
| `attached_garage_square_feet` | Garage space was associated with higher property value. |
| `porch_square_feet` | Outdoor living space showed a positive relationship with sale price. |
| `year_built` | Newer homes tended to have somewhat higher prices. |
| `has_waterfront_detail` | Waterfront details were associated with much higher prices, although rare. |
| `has_finished_space_detail` | Finished extra space added value across building-size groups. |
| `has_pool_or_spa_detail` | Pool/spa features were associated with higher prices, although rare. |
| `has_garage_or_carport_detail` | Garage/carport presence showed useful price differences. |
| `has_deck_or_porch_detail` | Deck/porch details were associated with higher median sale prices. |

```{r}
important_features <- c(
  "sale_price",
  "sale_year",
  "neighborhood",
  "latitude",
  "longitude",
  "square_feet",
  "quality",
  "bathrooms",
  "bedrooms",
  "land_net_square_feet",
  "attached_garage_square_feet",
  "porch_square_feet",
  "year_built",
  "has_waterfront_detail",
  "has_finished_space_detail",
  "has_pool_or_spa_detail",
  "has_garage_or_carport_detail",
  "has_deck_or_porch_detail"
)

joined_df <- joined_df %>%
  select(any_of(important_features))
final_analytics_df <- joined_df %>%
  distinct()

head(final_analytics_df,10)
```

# 22. Advanced EDA and Feature Engineering

After the main exploratory data analysis, additional derived features are created to better understand how sale price relates to size, quality, location, and selected property amenities.

The goal of this step is not only to inspect individual variables, but also to create more meaningful feature combinations. Some of these variables are useful for interpretation only, while others may later be useful for modeling.

Important note: variables that are calculated directly from `sale_price`, such as `price_per_sqft` and `price_category`, should not be used as predictors in the final regression model because they contain information from the target variable.

## 22.1 Starting Point: Final Analytics Dataset

The advanced EDA uses the final analytics dataset, which contains the most important features identified during the previous EDA steps.

```{r}
head(final_analytics_df, 10)
dim(final_analytics_df)
names(final_analytics_df)
```

## 22.2 Price per Square Foot

Price per square foot is created to normalize sale price by building size. This helps compare properties of different sizes and identify whether a property is expensive because it is large or because each square foot is highly valued.

This variable is useful for EDA, but it should not be used as a predictor in the final regression model because it is calculated using sale_price.

```{r}
final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    price_per_sqft = ifelse(
      !is.na(square_feet) & square_feet > 0,
      sale_price / square_feet,
      NA
    )
  )

summary(final_analytics_df$price_per_sqft)
ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(price_per_sqft), price_per_sqft > 0),
  aes(x = price_per_sqft)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Price per Square Foot",
    x = "Price per Square Foot in USD, Log Scale",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  )
```

The distribution of `price_per_sqft` is concentrated mostly around the middle range, with most properties falling roughly between 100 and 300 USD per square foot. The log scale helps reduce the influence of extreme values and makes the distribution easier to read.

The distribution is still slightly right-skewed, meaning that some properties have a much higher price per square foot than most others. These high values may represent very desirable locations, high-quality homes, waterfront properties, or unusual records.

## 22.3 Size-Based Features

Additional size-based features are created to measure property size more broadly. While square_feet captures the main building size, other areas such as porch space and garage space may also contribute to value.

```{r}
final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    total_extra_area = porch_square_feet + attached_garage_square_feet,
    total_size_score = square_feet + porch_square_feet + attached_garage_square_feet,
    building_to_land_ratio = ifelse(
      !is.na(land_net_square_feet) & land_net_square_feet > 0,
      square_feet / land_net_square_feet,
      NA
    )
  )
final_analytics_df %>%
  summarise(
    min_total_extra_area = min(total_extra_area, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_total_extra_area = median(total_extra_area, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_total_extra_area = mean(total_extra_area, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_total_extra_area = max(total_extra_area, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    min_total_size_score = min(total_size_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_total_size_score = median(total_size_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_total_size_score = mean(total_size_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_total_size_score = max(total_size_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    min_building_to_land_ratio = min(building_to_land_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_building_to_land_ratio = median(building_to_land_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_building_to_land_ratio = mean(building_to_land_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_building_to_land_ratio = max(building_to_land_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
p1 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(total_size_score), total_size_score > 0),
  aes(x = total_size_score, y = sale_price)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Sale Price vs Total Size Score",
    x = "Total Size Score, Log Scale",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale"
  )

p2 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(building_to_land_ratio), building_to_land_ratio > 0),
  aes(x = building_to_land_ratio, y = sale_price)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Sale Price vs Building-to-Land \nRatio",
    x = "Building-to-Land Ratio, Log Scale",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale"
  )

p1 + p2
```

The size-based features help capture different aspects of property size. total_size_score combines the main building area with porch and garage space, while building_to_land_ratio measures how much building area exists relative to the land area.

The size-based feature analysis shows that `total_size_score` has a clear positive relationship with `sale_price`. Properties with a higher total size score generally have higher sale prices. This confirms that combining building square footage with porch and attached garage area provides a useful broader measure of property size.

The `building_to_land_ratio` plot is less clear. Most properties are concentrated in a similar range, and the relationship with sale price is highly scattered. This suggests that the ratio between building size and land size does not explain sale price as clearly as the total size score. The ratio may still capture some property structure information, but it appears less important than direct size measures such as `square_feet` or `total_size_score`.

Overall, `total_size_score` appears useful for advanced EDA and potentially for modeling, while `building_to_land_ratio` should be treated as a weaker feature and reviewed later using model-based feature importance.

## 22.4 Quality Score

The quality variable is an ordered categorical feature. To make it easier to analyze and use in interaction features, it is converted into a numeric quality score 1-11.

```{r}
quality_order <- c(
  "Low",
  "Low Plus",
  "Fair",
  "Fair Plus",
  "Average",
  "Average Plus",
  "Good",
  "Good Plus",
  "Very Good",
  "Very Good Plus",
  "Excellent"
)

final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    quality_score = as.numeric(factor(
      quality,
      levels = quality_order,
      ordered = TRUE
    ))
  )

final_analytics_df %>%
  count(quality, quality_score) %>%
  arrange(quality_score)
final_analytics_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(quality_score), !is.na(sale_price)) %>%
  group_by(quality_score, quality) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = quality_score, y = median_sale_price)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Sale Price by Quality Score",
    x = "Quality Score",
    y = "Median Sale Price in USD"
  )
```

`quality_score` is a very useful derived feature because it converts the ordered quality categories into a numeric scale and shows a strong relationship with sale price.

## 22.5 Room Density Features

Bathroom and bedroom counts are useful, but their meaning depends on the size of the home. Room density features are created to measure how many bathrooms or bedrooms a property has relative to its building size.

```{r}
final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    bathrooms_per_1000_sqft = ifelse(
      !is.na(square_feet) & square_feet > 0,
      bathrooms / (square_feet / 1000),
      NA
    ),
    bedrooms_per_1000_sqft = ifelse(
      !is.na(square_feet) & square_feet > 0,
      bedrooms / (square_feet / 1000),
      NA
    )
  )
final_analytics_df %>%
  summarise(
    median_bathrooms_per_1000_sqft = median(bathrooms_per_1000_sqft, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bathrooms_per_1000_sqft = mean(bathrooms_per_1000_sqft, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bedrooms_per_1000_sqft = median(bedrooms_per_1000_sqft, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bedrooms_per_1000_sqft = mean(bedrooms_per_1000_sqft, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
p1 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(bathrooms_per_1000_sqft), bathrooms_per_1000_sqft > 0),
  aes(x = bathrooms_per_1000_sqft)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Bathrooms per 1,000 Square Feet",
    x = "Bathrooms per 1,000 Square Feet",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  )

p2 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(bedrooms_per_1000_sqft), bedrooms_per_1000_sqft > 0),
  aes(x = bedrooms_per_1000_sqft)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Bedrooms per 1,000 Square Feet",
    x = "Bedrooms per 1,000 Square Feet",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  )

p1 + p2
```

Bathroom and bedroom density are useful derived features because they adjust room counts for property size.

## 22.6 Interaction Features

The previous interaction analysis showed that sale price is affected by combinations of variables. Therefore, selected interaction features are created to capture combined effects between size, quality, location, and amenities.

```{r}
final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    square_feet_quality_interaction = square_feet * quality_score,
    bathrooms_quality_interaction = bathrooms * quality_score,
    finished_space_size_interaction = square_feet * as.numeric(has_finished_space_detail),
    garage_size_interaction = attached_garage_square_feet * as.numeric(has_garage_or_carport_detail),
    porch_size_interaction = porch_square_feet * as.numeric(has_deck_or_porch_detail),
    waterfront_land_interaction = land_net_square_feet * as.numeric(has_waterfront_detail)
  )
final_analytics_df %>%
  select(
    square_feet_quality_interaction,
    bathrooms_quality_interaction,
    finished_space_size_interaction,
    garage_size_interaction,
    porch_size_interaction,
    waterfront_land_interaction
  ) %>%
  summary()
p1 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(square_feet_quality_interaction), square_feet_quality_interaction > 0),
  aes(x = square_feet_quality_interaction, y = sale_price)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Sale Price vs Size-Quality \nInteraction",
    x = "Square Feet × Quality Score, Log Scale",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale"
  )

p2 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(bathrooms_quality_interaction), bathrooms_quality_interaction > 0),
  aes(x = bathrooms_quality_interaction, y = sale_price)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Sale Price vs Bathroom-Quality \nInteraction",
    x = "Bathrooms × Quality Score",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale"
  )

p3 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(finished_space_size_interaction), finished_space_size_interaction > 0),
  aes(x = finished_space_size_interaction, y = sale_price)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Sale Price vs Finished Space-Size \nInteraction",
    x = "Square Feet × Finished Space Detail, Log Scale",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale"
  )

p4 <- ggplot(
  final_analytics_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(waterfront_land_interaction), waterfront_land_interaction > 0),
  aes(x = waterfront_land_interaction, y = sale_price)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Sale Price vs Waterfront-Land \nInteraction",
    x = "Land Size × Waterfront Detail, Log Scale",
    y = "Sale Price in USD, Log Scale"
  )

(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
```

The interaction-feature plots show that several combined variables have meaningful relationships with sale price.

The `square_feet_quality_interaction` shows a positive relationship with sale price. Properties with larger building size and higher quality scores tend to have higher sale prices. This confirms that size and quality reinforce each other.

The `bathrooms_quality_interaction` also shows a positive relationship with sale price, although the plot is more concentrated. Homes with more bathrooms and higher quality scores tend to appear in higher price ranges.

The `finished_space_size_interaction` shows that properties with finished extra space and larger building size generally have higher sale prices. This supports the earlier finding that finished extra space adds value beyond the main square footage.

The `waterfront_land_interaction` is based on fewer observations because waterfront features are rare. However, the points appear mostly in higher price ranges, suggesting that waterfront-related land characteristics may contribute to higher property values.

Overall, these plots support the idea that interaction features can help capture combined effects between important variables. The most useful interaction features appear to be size-quality, bathroom-quality, finished-space-size, and waterfront-land interactions.

## 22.7 Location Clustering

Location is one of the most important drivers of property value. While neighborhood captures location as a categorical variable, latitude and longitude provide more precise geographic information. Location clusters are created using k-means clustering based on latitude and longitude.

```{r}
location_data <- final_analytics_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)) %>%
  select(latitude, longitude)

set.seed(123)

location_clusters <- kmeans(
  scale(location_data),
  centers = 10
)

final_analytics_df$location_cluster <- NA

final_analytics_df$location_cluster[
  !is.na(final_analytics_df$latitude) & !is.na(final_analytics_df$longitude)
] <- location_clusters$cluster

final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    location_cluster = as.factor(location_cluster)
  )
location_cluster_summary <- final_analytics_df %>%
  group_by(location_cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    median_sale_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_sale_price = mean(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(median_sale_price))

location_cluster_summary
ggplot(final_analytics_df, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = location_cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Location Clusters Based on Latitude and Longitude",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude",
    color = "Location Cluster"
  )
```

The location clustering analysis shows that properties can be grouped into clear geographic clusters using latitude and longitude. The clusters represent different spatial areas in the dataset and provide a more flexible way to capture location than using neighborhood codes alone.

The map shows that most clusters are geographically compact, meaning that the clustering successfully grouped nearby properties together. Some clusters cover larger or more spread-out areas, which may reflect rural or less densely populated regions.

Because location is one of the most important drivers of property value, these clusters may be useful for modeling. They can help capture regional price differences, especially when combined with other features such as building size, quality, and sale year.

```{r}
quality_order <- c(
  "Low",
  "Low Plus",
  "Fair",
  "Fair Plus",
  "Average",
  "Average Plus",
  "Good",
  "Good Plus",
  "Very Good",
  "Very Good Plus",
  "Excellent"
)

final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    quality = factor(quality, levels = quality_order, ordered = TRUE)
  )

quality_by_cluster <- final_analytics_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(location_cluster), !is.na(quality)) %>%
  count(location_cluster, quality) %>%
  group_by(location_cluster) %>%
  mutate(
    percent = n / sum(n) * 100
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(quality_by_cluster, aes(
  x = location_cluster,
  y = percent,
  fill = quality
)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Quality Distribution by Location Cluster",
    x = "Location Cluster",
    y = "Share of Properties",
    fill = "Quality"
  )
```

The quality distribution by location cluster shows that most clusters are dominated by `Average` and `Average Plus` quality properties. However, the share of higher-quality categories differs across clusters.

Some clusters, such as clusters 6 and 8, appear to contain a larger share of higher-quality properties compared with other clusters. This may partly explain why some location clusters have higher median sale prices. In contrast, clusters with a larger share of `Average`, `Fair`, or lower-quality properties may have lower median sale prices.

This suggests that location-based price differences are not only caused by geography itself, but may also be related to differences in property quality within each area. Therefore, both `location_cluster` and `quality_score` are useful features for modeling, and their interaction may also be important.

## 22.8 Location Price Multiplier

A location price multiplier is created by comparing the median sale price in each location cluster to the overall median sale price. A multiplier above 1 means that the cluster is more expensive than the overall median, while a multiplier below 1 means that the cluster is less expensive.

This variable is useful for interpretation. If used for modeling, it should be calculated only from the training data to avoid target leakage.

```{r}
overall_median_price <- median(final_analytics_df$sale_price, na.rm = TRUE)

location_price_multiplier <- final_analytics_df %>%
  group_by(location_cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    location_median_price = median(sale_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    location_price_multiplier = location_median_price / overall_median_price
  )

location_price_multiplier
final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  left_join(location_price_multiplier, by = "location_cluster")
ggplot(location_price_multiplier, aes(
  x = reorder(location_cluster, location_price_multiplier),
  y = location_price_multiplier
)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Location Price Multiplier by Cluster",
    x = "Location Cluster",
    y = "Location Price Multiplier"
  )
```

The location price multiplier confirms that geographic area strongly affects property value. Some clusters are clearly below the overall market median, while others are substantially above it.

## 22.9 Price Categories

Sale prices are grouped into lower, middle, and upper price categories based on quantiles. This is useful for interpretation and can support classification-style analysis, although the main prediction task remains regression.

```{r}
final_analytics_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  mutate(
    price_category = case_when(
      sale_price <= quantile(sale_price, 0.33, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Lower price",
      sale_price <= quantile(sale_price, 0.66, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Middle price",
      TRUE ~ "Upper price"
    )
  )

final_analytics_df %>%
  count(price_category)
final_analytics_df %>%
  count(price_category) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = price_category, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Properties by Price Category",
    x = "Price Category",
    y = "Number of Properties"
  )
```

The price categories divide the dataset into lower, middle, and upper price groups. This can help compare property characteristics across price levels.

## 22.10 Final Advanced EDA Dataset Check

After creating the advanced EDA features, the structure of the dataset is checked again.

```{r}
dim(final_analytics_df)
names(final_analytics_df)
advanced_missing_check <- data.frame(
  column_name = names(final_analytics_df),
  missing_count = sapply(final_analytics_df, function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  missing_percent = round(sapply(final_analytics_df, function(x) mean(is.na(x))) * 100, 2),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing_percent))

advanced_missing_check %>%
  filter(missing_count > 0)
```

## 22.11 Advanced EDA Summary

The advanced EDA extended the previous analysis by creating derived features that describe property value in a more detailed way. While the basic EDA showed which individual variables were related to `sale_price`, the advanced EDA helped explain how size, quality, location, and amenities work together.

First, `price_per_sqft` was created to normalize sale price by building size. This showed that most properties are concentrated around a typical price-per-square-foot range, while some properties have much higher values. These higher values may reflect premium locations, higher quality, waterfront features, or unusual properties. This feature is useful for interpretation, but it should not be used as a predictor because it is calculated from `sale_price`.

The size-based features provided additional insight into how property size can be measured. `total_size_score`, which combines building square footage, porch area, and attached garage area, showed a clear positive relationship with sale price. This suggests that overall usable or value-adding space matters beyond the main building square footage alone. In contrast, `building_to_land_ratio` showed a weaker and more scattered relationship, suggesting that direct size measures are more informative than the ratio between building size and land size.

The quality-score analysis confirmed that construction quality is one of the strongest drivers of sale price. By converting `quality` into an ordered numeric score, it became clear that median sale price increases as quality score increases. The increase is especially steep at the highest quality levels, suggesting that high-quality homes receive a strong market premium.

The room-density features gave a more detailed view of bathrooms and bedrooms. Instead of only counting rooms, `bathrooms_per_1000_sqft` and `bedrooms_per_1000_sqft` measure how many rooms a property has relative to its size. These features help identify homes with unusually high or low room density and may capture layout differences that simple room counts do not fully explain.

The interaction features showed that sale price is influenced by combinations of variables. The size-quality interaction showed that larger, higher-quality homes tend to have higher prices. The bathroom-quality interaction showed that the value of bathrooms depends partly on construction quality. The finished-space-size interaction confirmed that finished extra space adds value beyond main square footage. The waterfront-land interaction suggested that waterfront-related land characteristics may be associated with higher prices, although waterfront records are relatively rare.

The location clustering analysis added a more flexible way to represent geographic patterns. By clustering properties based on latitude and longitude, the dataset was divided into spatial groups. These clusters showed clear differences in median sale price, confirming that location strongly affects property value. The location price multiplier further showed that some clusters are below the overall market median, while others are substantially above it. This supports the idea that the same property characteristics can have different values depending on location.

Finally, price categories were created to divide properties into lower, middle, and upper price groups. These categories are useful for interpretation and comparison across market segments, but the main modeling task remains regression because `sale_price` is continuous.

Overall, the advanced EDA deepened the analysis by showing that the most important drivers of sale price are not only individual variables, but also derived measures and interactions.

### Most Important Insights from the Advanced EDA

| New feature | What it measures | Why it matters | Use for modeling? |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| `price_per_sqft` | Sale price divided by building square feet. | Helps compare properties after adjusting for size. It shows whether a property is expensive because it is large or because each square foot is highly valued. | No |
| `total_extra_area` | Combined porch area and attached garage area. | Captures additional usable or value-adding space beyond the main building size. | No |
| `total_size_score` | Main building square feet plus porch square feet plus attached garage square feet. | Gives a broader measure of total property space. It showed a clear positive relationship with sale price. | Yes |
| `building_to_land_ratio` | Building square feet divided by land square feet. | Measures how much of the land is developed. It can distinguish large parcels with small homes from more densely developed properties. | No |
| `quality_score` | Numeric version of the ordered `quality` variable. | Converts quality from categories into an ordered scale. It showed a strong positive relationship with median sale price. | Yes |
| `bathrooms_per_1000_sqft` | Number of bathrooms relative to building size. | Measures bathroom density instead of only bathroom count. It helps identify whether a home has many or few bathrooms for its size. | Yes |
| `bedrooms_per_1000_sqft` | Number of bedrooms relative to building size. | Measures bedroom density. It helps identify homes with unusually many or few bedrooms for their size. | Yes |
| `square_feet_quality_interaction` | Building size multiplied by quality score. | Captures the combined effect of size and quality. Large high-quality homes tend to have much higher prices. | Yes |
| `bathrooms_quality_interaction` | Number of bathrooms multiplied by quality score. | Captures whether bathrooms add more value in higher-quality properties. | Yes |
| `finished_space_size_interaction` | Building size multiplied by finished extra space indicator. | Captures whether finished extra space adds value differently depending on home size. | Yes |
| `garage_size_interaction` | Attached garage square feet multiplied by garage/carport indicator. | Combines garage size with garage/carport presence. | No |
| `porch_size_interaction` | Porch square feet multiplied by deck/porch indicator. | Combines outdoor area size with deck/porch presence. | No |
| `waterfront_land_interaction` | Land size multiplied by waterfront indicator. | Captures whether land size behaves differently when waterfront-related features are present. | Yes |
| `location_cluster` | Geographic cluster based on latitude and longitude. | Groups nearby properties together and captures spatial price patterns beyond neighborhood codes. | Yes |
| `location_price_multiplier` | Median price of each location cluster divided by the overall median price. | Shows whether a location cluster is above or below the overall market median. | No |
| `price_category` | Lower, middle, or upper price group based on sale price quantiles. | Helps compare properties across price segments. | No |

# 23. Final Feature selection

Because the final goal is to build a user-facing price prediction app, the modeling features were reduced to variables that a user can realistically provide or that the app can derive automatically. Technical assessor variables and highly specific categorical codes were removed from the app-focused feature set. This improves usability and ensures that the model can be used in a real prediction interface.

```{r}
app_model_features <- c(
  "sale_price",

  # time
  "sale_year",

  # location
  "latitude",
  "longitude",
  "location_cluster",

  # size
  "square_feet",
  "land_net_square_feet",
  "total_size_score",

  # quality
  "quality_score",

  # rooms
  "bathrooms",
  "bedrooms",
  "bathrooms_per_1000_sqft",
  "bedrooms_per_1000_sqft",

  # property age
  "year_built",

  # amenities
  "has_garage_or_carport_detail",
  "has_deck_or_porch_detail",
  "has_finished_space_detail",
  "has_pool_or_spa_detail",
  "has_waterfront_detail",

  # interactions
  "square_feet_quality_interaction",
  "bathrooms_quality_interaction",
  "finished_space_size_interaction",
  "waterfront_land_interaction"
)

app_model_df <- final_analytics_df %>%
  select(any_of(app_model_features)) %>%
  distinct()
```

For the App input form, users should add the following information:

| App input | Used to create model features |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Address or map location | `latitude`, `longitude`, `location_cluster` - will be derived |
| Sale year | `sale_year` |
| Living area | `square_feet` |
| Land size | `land_net_square_feet` |
| Porch/deck yes/no | `has_deck_or_porch_detail` |
| Porch/deck size | `porch_square_feet` |
| Garage yes/no | `has_garage_or_carport_detail` |
| Garage size | `attached_garage_square_feet` |
| Quality rating | `quality_score` |
| Number of bedrooms | `bedrooms`, `bedrooms_per_1000_sqft` - will be derived |
| Number of bathrooms | `bathrooms`, `bathrooms_per_1000_sqft` - will be derived |
| Year built | `year_built` |
| Pool/spa yes/no | `has_pool_or_spa_detail` |
| Waterfront yes/no | `has_waterfront_detail` |
| Finished extra space yes/no | `has_finished_space_detail` |
